summary: Sunil Pai from Cloudflare introduces "Code Mode," a paradigm where AI models generate executable JavaScript code instead of relying on traditional JSON-based tool calling. Tool calling works for small-scale use cases but breaks when hundreds of tools fill the context window, creating slow back-and-forth exchanges. Models are already trained on vast amounts of code, so generating JavaScript leverages existing capabilities. Code provides typed APIs, type checking, syntax error detection, looping, state holding, sequencing, and parallelization in a single execution. Cloudflare applied this to their API surface of approximately 2,600 endpoints. Exposing every endpoint as a tool would consume 1.2 million tokens. Colleague Matt Carey's solution: expose just two tools—search and execute—both accepting code strings, reducing to 1,000 tokens (99.9% reduction). Pai demonstrates with a "mythical server" demo where a DDoS-mitigation prompt generates and executes code in one shot. He shares Kenton's tic-tac-toe canvas anecdote: the model inspected canvas state (an array of strokes), recognized the game pattern, and played by drawing strokes—"inhabiting the state machine" rather than generating a separate program. This leads to the "Harness" architecture: a sandboxed execution environment starting with zero capabilities, with capabilities granted explicitly via capability-based security using V8 isolates. Pai extends this to long-running workflows that persist for days, months, or years with state, and generative UI where every user gets a perfectly custom interface generated on the fly—solving the e-commerce problem where popularity forces bland one-size-fits-all UIs. He notes the harness can run closer to the user, stitching together different services in a safe, task-by-task environment. Pai envisions the next billion users as agents that "dream in types and syntax errors," requiring rethought developer experiences: markdown docs, errors that guide agents, and discoverability via search. He argues capability-based security enables a safe "eval" that reopens a tech tree unexplored for 30 years. The distinction between programmers (who had infinite power via code) and everyone else (who got buttons and forms) is breaking—code is now the universal interface to all systems.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker background
sections.summary: Sunil Pai is introduced as creator of PartyKit and AI agent builder at Cloudflare. He frames the talk as being about "Code Mode," noting prior art exists but focusing on its implications.

sections.title: Limitations of traditional tool calling at scale
sections.summary: Tool calling works with few tools but breaks when hundreds of tools (Google services, Jira, wiki) fill the context window. Composition is weird and back-and-forth with the model is slow.

sections.title: The shift to generating executable code
sections.summary: Instead of JSON back-and-forth, the model generates JavaScript to run against an environment. Benefits include typed APIs, type checking, syntax errors, and fundamental code capabilities like looping, state, sequencing, and parallelization in a single execution.

sections.title: Scaling API usage at Cloudflare
sections.summary: Cloudflare's 2,600 API endpoints would require 1.2 million tokens as individual tools. Matt Carey's solution: two tools (search and execute) accepting code strings. Search takes the OpenAPI JSON spec; execute provides callable functions. Reduced to 1,000 tokens—99.9% reduction. DDoS mitigation example shows code running next to API surface in one shot.

sections.title: Live demonstration of the Mythical server
sections.summary: Live demo attempting to list workers via the mythical server. The model searches for API endpoints, generates code, and executes requests. Demo had on-stage rendering issues but showed the workflow: search for endpoints, generate code, execute in one run.

sections.title: A new way of interacting with systems
sections.summary: LLMs break the boundary between programmers (who write scripts) and non-technical users (who rely on pre-built apps). Every person now has a buddy that generates and executes code against exposed systems, safely.

sections.title: The Kenton canvas and tic-tac-toe anecdote
sections.summary: Kenton (Cloudflare Workers creator) built a canvas environment and drew a tic-tac-toe board. When asked to play, the model tried generating a tic-tac-toe app; Kenton redirected it to inspect the state (array of strokes). The model recognized the board and played by drawing strokes—no tic-tac-toe code existed in the system. Pai calls this "inhabiting the state machine" rather than generating a program. Notably, Opus let Kenton win.

sections.title: New software architecture: The Harness
sections.summary: Everyone is building a "harness"—a general-purpose computing environment that generates code and executes it in a sandbox. Unlike containers that start with capabilities and are secured from outside, this sandbox starts with zero capabilities: no fetches, no APIs. Capabilities are granted explicitly. Cloudflare uses V8 isolates for fast startup and 10 years of security hardening. Default recommendation: no outgoing fetches, only APIs.

sections.title: Observability and long-running workflows
sections.summary: Pai emphasizes the need for absolute full observability into sandboxed execution—you must be able to trace why the system made a specific action on a past date. V8 isolates, WebAssembly, or custom JavaScript interpreters all work; the key is fast execution with exposed capabilities. From here, ambitions expand to long-running workflows that persist for days, months, or years, each carrying state through its lifetime.

sections.title: Generative UI and custom programs per user
sections.summary: In a world of generative UI, perfectly custom UIs can be generated for every user. E-commerce exemplifies the problem: popularity forces bland one-size-fits-all interfaces. With Code Mode, you generate completely different programs backed by your backend for each user—e.g., returning shoes and finding similar items under $100, or checking a delayed order—each a custom generated program rather than a pre-built feature.

sections.title: Running the harness closer to the user
sections.summary: People find power running the harness closer to the user (e.g., on an iPhone) to mash up different services in a safe, task-by-task environment. Pai jokes it's an anti-Cloudflare talk since users should run software on their devices, not Cloudflare servers, but the point is stitching systems together safely.

sections.title: Rethinking UI and the next billion users as agents
sections.summary: Pai frames Code Mode as reopening a tech tree unexplored for 30 years because eval wasn't safe—now it is. The next billion users of systems are agents that 'dream in types and syntax errors.' Developer experience for agents matters: markdown docs, errors that guide agents, discoverability via search. Capability-based security is language-agnostic (Python, WASM, even Lisp). UI programmers may adapt particularly well given their proximity to users.

sections.title: Conclusion: Let the code do the talking
sections.summary: Pai concludes that programmers historically had infinite power via code while everyone else got buttons and forms. That distinction is breaking. In this new world, code is the universal interface to all systems. He invites discussion and finishes with 6 seconds remaining.
